## Agenda

- Why human review remains essential
- Techniques for evaluating AI-generated outputs
- Building a validation checklist

## Human in the loop is not new

- The underlying reason for keeping a human in the loop is not new. We have done this for a long time. When the output came from a human, we might have called it "TTL-in-the-loop", or simply good old-fashioned `review`.

- Whoever is responsible for the final output, whether it was generated by AI or produced by a junior human team member, is ultimately accountable for its quality and accuracy.

- As with a skilled STC, the TTL soon learns what needs to be reviewed and what can safely be delegated without close review.

- We all know this principle, so I do not need to justify it further. The rest of this presentation is about how to review AI outputs and safely delegate tasks to computers for independent execution.

## Reduce the need before addressing it

- Computers have been handling important tasks for decades, including managing retirement funds.
- No one manually manages every financial transaction.
- So, what is different about AI-powered computers?
- AI is non-deterministic: its output can vary. If the code behind financial transactions behaved randomly, those transactions would also require human oversight.
- AI's non-deterministic nature is also useful. It is central to generative AI, which has opened up opportunities for computers to perform qualitative tasks they could not handle before. This is amazing and will revolutionize the world in ways we still cannot understand in 2026.

## In practice

- Today's AI systems can take on complex workflows and handle them non-deterministically. They work well for the vast majority of use cases.
- If "the vast majority of use cases" is not good enough for your task, you need a human in the loop.
- But before configuring a human-in-the-loop system, can we reduce the need for one?

- Many tasks can be handled reliably by deterministic code. This is how we manage financial transactions and why you can transfer money through online banking even when no one is on shift.

- To reduce the need for a human in the loop, first ask whether you can break your workflow into smaller tasks. Then consider which tasks are better suited to deterministic code.



- The first step in setting up a human-in-the-loop system is to reduce the need for human intervention as much as possible.

## But I can't code!?

- Maybe you can't code, but the agent can do it for you!

- Creating the code requires a human in the loop. You need to validate that it performs the intended tasks. This takes time during setup, but the workflow can then run automatically each time.

- How can I verify code if I can't code?

  - After the code has been written, ask the agent to explain what it does. Use different models to check whether the explanations are consistent and accurate.
  - Ask the agent to explain in a language you understand, such as plain English. Keep asking questions until you are confident.
  - Give the agent test cases, including tricky ones that check how it handles edge cases. Don't use only easy or obvious examples; real-world examples aren't always easy or obvious.

## Break up the workflow further

- After identifying tasks that can be handled deterministically by code, ask whether the remaining tasks can be split into smaller ones.
- The more complex a task is, the harder it is to write a single instruction that handles it well.
- Some tasks may be made small and simple enough for AI to handle reliably without human intervention. But until we are AI experts, we may not know in advance which tasks those are. We can learn by monitoring how the system performs.
- To set yourself up to need as little human oversight as possible, break tasks into smaller prompts instead of relying on "one prompt to rule them all."

## Bridge to regular prompting

- What I have described here is more like a multi-agent workflow. Since we do not yet have platforms at the WB where this is easy to set up, we have not included it in the training. But it is coming with Claude, especially Claude Cowork.

- Until then, we can still apply these ideas to regular agentic prompting, such as with GitHub Copilot.

- If possible, do one task at a time instead of writing one gigantic prompt.

## So how is this actually done?

- In code agents in VS Code, we are asked to approve each edit. That is straightforward.

- For more complex workflows, there is no equivalent way to stay in the loop, because workflows vary.

- General principles:

  - Have each step, whether code-based or non-deterministic, save both its final output and its work.
  - Set milestones where you review the outputs and the work for correctness.
  - Use a review agent to review each step and classify cases as certain or uncertain. Then have a human review only the uncertain cases. Without this gatekeeping step, an agent will do its best at each step and move on to the next. The review step should prevent a case from progressing until a human confirms it is correct.

- You probably have more intuition for how to do this than you think. If you have ever managed a junior team member, you already have an intuition for what to review and what to delegate.
